props.command: I need to track 50 AI vendors, their filings, code, research, and news. Build me a pipeline that turns all that public signal into one scored brief per company, on demand.

beats.narration_text: This is Muskan, in for Humanitarians AI. Picture tracking fifty AI vendors at once, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Mistral, all of them. Nobody reads every filing, repo, and press release by hand. So I built a pipeline that does, and today we open it up: public signal in, one honest brief out.

items fly along a drawn connector toward center

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole shape. Five public sources feed the collectors. Everything they find collapses into one thing, a scored signal, landing in a single table. You ask for a company by name, and the system reads its strongest signals back as a brief. Public data in, brief out. Nothing private, nothing behind a login.

show.event: five chips light in narration order
chip 2 emphasizes on 'is the code alive'

items: SEC EDGAR — filings, revenue, exec changes
props.caption: five sources, five questions

beats.narration_text: The collectors pull five sources, and each answers a different question. SEC EDGAR: the money, revenue and executive changes, public companies only. GitHub: is the code alive, stars, commits, releases. ArXiv: real research, by affiliation. Google News: funding, layoffs, partnerships. And a hand-seeded Neo4j graph for who competes with whom.

show.event: a raw finding card morphs into a signal row
importance score counter fills to a value (accent)
the row drops into the ai_company_signals stack

layers.title: ai_company_signals
layers.sub: one row per signal, in Postgres

beats.narration_text: Here's the decision that makes it work. Every finding, a filing, a release, a headline, becomes the same shape: a signal. It gets a type, from funding to executive change to product launch, and an importance score, zero to one hundred. Different sources, one table, one ruler. Now you can rank noise by what actually matters.

show.event: two company nodes appear and draw a COMPETES_WITH edge
a BACKED_BY edge draws to an investor node (accent)
a small 'hand-seeded' caption fades in under the graph

props.caption: Neo4j — the relationships filings can't give you (hand-seeded)

beats.note: A bespoke graph illustration (two nodes + drawn COMPETES_WITH / BACKED_BY edges) reads better than ChipGrid here; slate it and build a reel-local comp, or drop a Manim graph scene into scenes.py. ChipGrid is the fallback.
beats.narration_text: Filings tell you what a company did. They don't tell you who it's up against. That lives in a graph, companies linked by competes-with, and to the investors that back them. It's seeded by hand, which is the honest catch: the graph is only as current as the last time a person updated it.

layers.title: log tokens + cost

props.caption: built to run cheap, every day

beats.narration_text: Now the payoff. You send one company name. Same day, already asked? It serves a cached brief, free. Otherwise it pulls the top signals, writes the brief, and logs the exact tokens and cost of doing it. That cost line is the point: you always know what each answer cost, so this is a tool you can actually afford to run every day.

artifactLines: What it is: 5 public sources → one scored-signal table → an on-demand, cost-tracked brief per company.
The design tell: every finding becomes a 0–100 signal, so noise ranks by what matters.
Where it's strong: public-only and auditable — every brief traces back to a signal row.
Where it bites: public signals lag reality, scores are heuristics, and the competitor graph is only as fresh as its last hand-edit.

beats.narration_text: Five sources, one scored table, one cheap brief on demand. The strength is honesty: it's all public, and every line traces to a signal row you can check. The catch, said plainly: public data lags, the scores are judgment calls, and the graph is hand-seeded. Know that, and it's a real tool. Forget it, and you'll trust it too much.

props.command: For [company], pull the last quarter of public signals — filings, GitHub activity, research, news. Score each 0–100 by importance, name the single most important one, and list what you could NOT verify from public sources.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt and point it at a vendor you actually care about. It asks Claude to pull last quarter's public signals, score each one, flag the single most important, and, crucially, list what it could not verify. That last part matters: an honest answer names its own blind spots. Run it, and read the gaps as closely as the findings.
